title: What is the difference between array and linked list: array has fast access by index O(1) but slow insert/delete; linked list has slow access O(n) but fast insert/delete at head O(1).
shortTitle: What is the difference between array and linked list
keyPoints: An array stores elements in contiguous memory, giving O(1) random access by index but O(n) insertion or deletion in the middle.
A linked list stores elements as scattered nodes connected by references, giving O(n) access but O(1) insertion at a known position.
Arrays have better cache locality because contiguous memory is loaded into CPU cache together.
Linked lists avoid costly resizing and shifting, growing one node at a time.
In Java, ArrayList is backed by an array and LinkedList is a doubly linked list.
For most workloads ArrayList wins in practice due to cache locality; LinkedList is used mainly for frequent insertions and removals at both ends.

s1_definition.oneliner: Array gives fast index access but slow middle insert; linked list gives slow access but fast head insert.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Array** – stores elements in one contiguous block of memory, giving O(1) random access by index but O(n) insertion or deletion because elements must shift.
- **Linked list** – stores elements as scattered nodes connected by references, giving O(n) access because you must traverse, but O(1) insertion or deletion at a known position.
- **Cache locality** – arrays benefit from contiguous memory loading; linked lists suffer cache misses.
- **Resizing** – arrays must be copied to a larger block when full; linked lists grow one node at a time.
- **Java implementations** – `ArrayList` is backed by an array; `LinkedList` is a doubly linked list.
s1_definition.analogy: An array is like a row of numbered lockers at National Bank of India bolted side by side: Rajesh can jump straight to locker five instantly, but to squeeze a new locker into the middle every later locker must be unbolted and moved. A linked list is like a treasure hunt where each clue points to the next hiding spot: adding a new clue at the start is trivial, but to reach the fifth clue you must follow the first four.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The core difference between an array and a linked list is how they store data and the performance trade-off that follows. An array stores its elements in one contiguous block of memory, so I can jump to any index instantly by computing a memory offset, which gives constant-time random access. A linked list stores its elements as separate nodes scattered across the heap, each pointing to the next, so to reach a particular position I must start at the head and follow the chain.

The trade-off flips for insertion and deletion. Inserting into the middle of an array forces every element after the insertion point to shift, which is linear time. Inserting at the head of a linked list is constant time because I only re-point one reference.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I choose the structure based on the workload. For reading a transaction at a specific position in a statement I use an array-backed structure because the constant-time index access is exactly what I need. For a queue of newly arriving transactions I use a linked structure because the constant-time head insertion avoids any shifting.

The last point I always make is cache locality: because an array is contiguous, iterating it is fast since the CPU pulls neighbouring elements into cache together, whereas a linked list suffers cache misses. That is why in practice an ArrayList usually outperforms a LinkedList for iteration.

Remember one sentence: arrays win on access and cache locality, linked lists win on insertion at known positions, and for most Java workloads ArrayList is the default.
